Q: Google Play rejection: How to handle required permanent data retention for an Android app without MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE? A:

If it needs to survive uninstall, MANAGE_EXTERNAL_STORAGE won't help anyway. It doesn't do what you think it does (it doesn't store it to an SD card). And even data stored in external storage is deleted on uninstall and clearing data. Back it up to a server. You might be able to get away with just Google's autobackup depending on if the user has it on, size of data, etc. But really the right answer here is to use a server to store the backups.

Storing the db to a public folder is a horrible idea. For one, it shouldn't be possible for most folders. For another, it means any other app can overwrite your data accidentally or maliciously. Or the user could do it accidentally while cleaning up files on their phone. It's a really bad idea.

Q: GCC miscompiles long chains of overloaded `operator,` A:

This is due to raw_data_min_len being set to 128(which act as a threshold) in Speed up compilation of large char array initializers when not using #embed.

The following patch (again, on top of the #embed patchset attempts to optimize compilation of large {{{,un}signed ,}char,std::byte} array initializers when not using #embed in the source.

Unlike the C patch which is done during the parsing of initializers this is done when lexing tokens into an array, because C++ lexes all tokens upfront and so by the time we parse the initializers we already have 16 bytes per token allocated (i.e. 32 extra compile time memory bytes per one byte in the array).

The drawback is again that it can result in worse locations for diagnostics (-Wnarrowing, -Wconversion) when initializing signed char arrays with values 128..255. Not really sure what to do about this though unlike the C case, the locations would need to be preserved through reshape_init* and perhaps till template instantiation.

For #embed, there is just a single location_t (could be range of the directive), for diagnostics perhaps we could extend it to say byte xyz of the file embedded here or something like that, but the optimization done by this patch, either we'd need to bump the minimum limit at which to try it, or say temporarily allocate a location_t array for each byte and then clear it when we no longer need it or something. ... 2025-01-21 Jakub Jelinek jakub@redhat.com

Q: Dynamic Array searchable Data Validation A:

As per the following screenshot. D6:E14 are the items list. Helper dynamic formulas-

H6=TRANSPOSE(UNIQUE(E6:.E100))
H7=DROP(REDUCE("",H6#,LAMBDA(a,x,IFNA(HSTACK(a,FILTER(D6:.D100,E6:.E1100=x)),""))),,1)

Then put this formula =$H$6# in A1 data validation list source. And this formula =INDEX($H$7:.$J$100,,MATCH($A1,$H$6#,0)). Drag down dropdown cells. You are all setup.

Q: Can I access my Apple Music library via API from a generic Python script? A:

The Short Answer

You can do this from Python, but Apple makes it deliberately difficult for non-Apple-platform apps. Here's why:

The Authentication Challenge

Apple Music API requires two tokens:

  1. Developer Token - A JWT you generate from your Apple Developer account credentials. This is straightforward and works from any platform.

  2. Music User Token - This is where it gets tricky. This token authorizes access to a specific user's library (yours), and Apple's official flows for obtaining it are designed around either native Apple apps (MusicKit for Swift) or web apps (MusicKit JS in a browser).

What "MusicKit on the Web" Actually Means

The code examples you saw are JavaScript, specifically designed to run in a browser. MusicKit JS handles the OAuth-like flow where:

  1. User clicks "Connect to Apple Music"

  2. Browser opens Apple's auth popup

  3. User signs in and grants permission

  4. MusicKit JS receives the Music User Token

This is inherently browser-based because Apple wants to ensure the user is actually present and consenting.

Your Options for Python

Option 1: Hybrid Approach (Most Reliable)

Use a browser-based flow once to get a Music User Token, then use that token in your Python scripts. The token is long-lived (though it does expire). You could:

  • Set up a minimal local web server in Python

  • Open a browser to Apple's auth flow

  • Capture the token when it redirects back

  • Save it for use in subsequent API calls

Option 2: Reverse Engineering (Fragile)

Some people have extracted tokens from the Apple Music web player by inspecting network requests after logging in. This works but violates ToS and can break anytime.

Option 3: Use Shortcuts/Automation on macOS

If you have a Mac, you could use Apple Shortcuts or AppleScript to interact with the Music app directly, bypassing the API entirely.
